prose.def: A vision or supernatural sight in which something normally unseen comes into view.
prose.article: ὀπτασία refers to a vision—something supernatural that appears to a person's sight, like Zechariah's experience in the temple or Paul's heavenly vision. All four times it occurs in the New Testament, translators render it "vision" with complete agreement. The older lexicon Abbott-Smith notes a broader basic idea of "an appearing" or "coming into view," which shows up in some Septuagint passages, but in the New Testament the meaning consistently narrows to a supernatural vision.
prose.caution: The word is relatively rare (only 4 New Testament uses and 2 in the Septuagint), so its full range rests on limited evidence.

receipts.how: Zechariah's speechlessness after leaving the temple is explained by his having seen a vision (ὀπτασία), directly exemplifying the supernatural-sight meaning the definition gives.

audit.author_note: Luke (Gospel and Acts) frames ὀπτασία within narrative accounts of divine encounters, while Paul (2 Cor 12:1) uses it in a polemical context defending his apostolic credentials, but neither usage departs from the core sense of a supernatural vision.

prose.def: An adjective meaning roasted, broiled, or (in non-biblical usage) baked, describing food or material prepared by direct heat.
senseLabels: roasted or broiled (describing food cooked over heat)
prose.article: ὀπτός is a simple adjective meaning "cooked by fire," whether roasted, broiled, or baked. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:42, where the risen Jesus is given a piece of broiled fish, and twice in the Septuagint at Exodus 12, both times rendering the Hebrew צָלִי (roasted) for the Passover lamb. The everyday flavor of the word shines through in the papyri, where it shows up in a feast shopping-list as ὀπτοῦ δέλφακος, "roast pork," and very commonly with bricks (ὀπτὸς πλίνθος, "baked brick").
prose.caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use and two in the Septuagint — though the meaning is well confirmed by papyri and lexica.

prose.def: Late summer as a season, and by extension the ripe fruit of that period; used metaphorically in its single NT occurrence (REV 18:14).
senseLabels: ripe fruit (metonymy for the late-summer season)
prose.article: ὀπώρα originally named the season of late summer and early autumn—roughly late July through early September—and by extension came to mean the ripe fruit of that time. In its single New Testament appearance (Revelation 18:14) it refers to fruit, though the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering here is tied to the phrase 'the fruit your soul longed for.' A nice everyday parallel comes from an Egyptian tax-gatherer's first-century letter, where he complains 'there has not been much fruit in Memphis up to the present,' showing the word was common, ordinary Koine.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

prose.def: A conjunction meaning 'in order that' or 'so that' introducing purpose or reported requests, and occasionally a relative adverb meaning 'how' or 'as.'
prose.article: ὅπως is a little connecting word that almost never gets translated as a standalone English word — in 56 of its 57 New Testament appearances it disappears into the phrasing, doing its work as part of a clause. Its core job is to introduce purpose ("in order that," "so that"), and it also follows verbs of asking or urging to report a request. The Septuagint uses it 170 times, most often to render the Hebrew מַ֫עַן ("for the sake of, so that") 83 times, which lines up neatly with its purpose-driven meaning; everyday Koine papyri show the same range, including one document where it functions almost like "so let it be given."
prose.caution: Older lexicons note a rarer use of ὅπως meaning "how" or "as" (as in Luke 24:20), so the word's range is slightly broader than its dominant purpose sense suggests.

prose.def: Something seen; either a supernatural vision or divine communication (most NT uses) or a remarkable sight or spectacle witnessed in waking experience.
senseLabels: 1. a supernatural vision or divine communication
prose.article: ὅραμα is literally "that which is seen," and in the New Testament it nearly always refers to a vision—a supernatural sight, often granted in sleep or a trance. Of its 12 occurrences, 8 (73%) are rendered "vision," and the word clusters heavily in Acts, where figures like Cornelius and Paul receive divine messages this way. In the Septuagint it appears 41 times, frequently translating the Hebrew חָזוֹן ("vision"), and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one third-century BC letter and a temple inscription both speak of a ὅραμα as a vision experienced in sleep.

prose.def: A sight or divinely given vision; often used adverbially to describe how something appears, especially in apocalyptic imagery.
senseLabels: appearance — like (adverbial comparison, same verse as sense 2)
how the vision appeared (appearance of a vision)
prose.article: ὅρασις covers a range from the basic act of seeing to the way something appears and, further, to a God-given vision. The four New Testament uses split evenly between "appearance" (how something looked, as in Revelation 4:3) and "vision" (an inspired sight, as in Acts 2:17 and Revelation 9:17), and the Septuagint uses it 91 times, mostly for Hebrew words meaning "appearance" (מַרְאֶה) or "vision" (חָזוֹן). A striking piece of evidence: an inscription records Stratia offering a gift to the goddess Demeter "on account of restored sight," showing the plain, everyday sense of physical seeing.
prose.caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, the measured senses overlap heavily, and how to split a single verse like Revelation 4:3 between "appearance" and "vision" is somewhat arbitrary.

prose.def: To see physically or perceive mentally; also used as a command to look or take heed, and in passive form to mean 'appear' or 'be seen.'
prose.article: ὁράω is the basic verb for seeing, used 657 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "saw" in 88% of cases. Beyond physical sight it stretches to mental perception ("discern") and to warnings like "take heed" or "beware"—in fact Moulton-Milligan note the word is cognate with our English "be ware." prose.caution: Note that in everyday Koine the present tense was rare, its place often taken by βλέπω and θεωρέω, so ὁράω commonly appears in its aorist and other forms.

prose.def: Describing a person habitually inclined to anger; irascible or prone to losing one's temper.
prose.article: ὀργίλος describes a person who is easily provoked to anger — hot-tempered or irascible. It appears only once in the New Testament (Titus 1:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "quick"), but the Septuagint uses it 4 times, twice translating Hebrew words for wrath or fury (Proverbs 22:24; 29:22). A notable parallel comes from the Didache (iii.2), which warns "do not be ὀργίλος, for anger leads to murder," capturing exactly the sense found in the classical lexica.
prose.caution: This is a New Testament hapax, so its precise range there rests on a single verse plus the broader Septuagint and Koine evidence.

prose.def: A fathom, a unit of depth equal to the span of a person's outstretched arms, about five or six feet.
prose.article: This word names a fathom — the distance measured by your outstretched arms, used here for sounding the depth of water beneath a ship. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in the same verse (Acts 27:28), where sailors measure the sea depth as they near land. An ancient measurement papyrus (P Oxy IV.669) helpfully defines it as 4 cubits, calling it "the distance of the outstretched hands," which matches the word's link to the verb meaning to reach out.
prose.caution: Both occurrences are in a single verse, and the two "measured senses" simply reflect different wordings for the same nautical depth measurement.

prose.def: (middle voice) To reach out after or long for something (with genitive), whether a worthy goal, a destructive craving, or an eschatological hope.
prose.article: ὀρέγομαι pictures someone literally stretching out to grasp something, used figuratively to mean reaching after, longing for, or aspiring to a goal. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament (1 Timothy 3:1 and 6:10, Hebrews 11:16), and in each case it is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word. Interestingly, in everyday papyri and inscriptions the related forms could mean simply 'to come to someone's assistance' or 'reach out a helping hand,' showing how the basic idea of stretching out could go beyond mere desire.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament and is always absorbed into phrasing, so its precise force in each passage is hard to pin down.

prose.def: An adjective meaning mountainous or hilly; used as a noun (the hill country) in both NT occurrences (Luke 1:39, 65), referring to the highlands of Judea.
prose.article: ὀρεινός is an adjective meaning "mountainous" or "hilly," built from ὄρος (mountain). In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Luke 1 (verses 39 and 65), where it functions as a noun for "the hill country" of Judea. The word was common in everyday Koine: the papyri regularly use it to describe canals along the edge of the desert, and in the Septuagint it occurs 17 times, often rendering the Hebrew שְׁפֵלָה (lowland).
prose.caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a confidence tier of low, both uses are the same noun phrase, so the apparent two senses reflect translation wording rather than distinct meanings.

prose.def: A general word for desire, longing, or appetite; used in the New Testament once (Romans 1:27) of inflamed sexual craving.

The most striking evidence comes from the papyri: an imprecatory tablet from Hadrumetum reads "I adjure thee, demonic spirit... by the God of Abraham," matching exactly how the demon-possessed man uses the word against Jesus in Mark 5:7. In the Septuagint it appears 27 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew verb for swearing an oath (שָׁבַע, 22 times).
prose.caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences split across two senses, the precise English range rests on thin measured evidence.

prose.def: A sworn oath—any solemn vow or binding declaration, whether a human promise, legal pledge, or divine guarantee, often invoking God as witness.
prose.article: Ὅρκος means an oath: a formal, binding promise sworn before God or witnesses. Its range is narrow and consistent—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "oath" in 7 of 10 New Testament occurrences (70%), and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100% of the time, with the few other renderings still revolving around swearing or promising. The everyday Koine papyri show the same usage: one third-century BC document reads "I swore to you the ancestral oath beside the river," while others mention "the customary oath" in farm leases and deeds of sale—an oath was simply part of ordinary legal life. In the Septuagint it appears 42 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for an oath (25×).

prose.def: To move suddenly and forcefully in a direction — to rush or charge toward a place or person, always intransitive in the New Testament.
prose.article: ὁρμάω describes a sudden, forceful surge of motion — people, animals, or crowds dashing toward a place or target. In all 5 New Testament occurrences it works the same way: a herd of pigs plunging down a slope, or an angry mob charging at someone. The everyday papyri show the same flavor, where people "took to flight" (εἰς φυγὴν ὥρμησαν), though one later document weakens it to simply going after something you wanted. The three "senses" measured here are really one core meaning of rushing, just colored by what's added — "whole," "together," or alone.
prose.caution: With only 5 occurrences, the distinctions between the measured senses reflect translation phrasing rather than truly separate meanings.

prose.def: A forceful impulse or rush — either a hostile assault by a crowd or the driving impulse that directs something, as a rudder follows a pilot's intent.
senseLabels: a driving impulse that directs movement
prose.article: ὁρμή names a forceful movement, but the New Testament's two uses pull in two directions: in Acts 14:5 it is a hostile rush — an attempt set in motion to attack — while in James 3:4 it is the impulse or drive by which a pilot steers a ship. The Septuagint uses it seven times across four books, and everyday Koine papyri show the same range, from soldiers repelling an enemy's onset to two pigs "making a rush" onto someone's land. The classical lexica reflect both meanings, listing a violent movement or impulse alongside a hostile assault.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences split evenly between two different senses, the evidence is thin and the word's range here is hard to pin down.

Long thought to be the only instance in Biblical or secular Greek, it has since turned up in an inscription from Priene (after 133 B.C.) referring to a Rhodian judgment and "delimitation," confirming that everyday Koine used it for marking off territory.

prose.def: A relative (and occasionally demonstrative) pronoun meaning who, which, what, or that, linking a clause to a previously mentioned person or thing.
prose.article: ὅς is the standard Koine relative pronoun, usually translated "who," "which," "what," or "that" depending on what it points back to. It is extraordinarily common, appearing 1,408 times in the New Testament, and its exact English form shifts so much with context that 730 of those occurrences get absorbed into the phrasing with no single English word of their own. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly stands in for the Hebrew relative particle אֲשֶׁר, used 2,918 times that way. Notably, the lexica also document an older demonstrative use ("the one... the other"), confirmed in everyday papyri, as in a complaint of assault from A.D. 38.
prose.caution: Because this is a grammatical connector, the measured "senses" are really translation forms driven by surrounding words, not distinct meanings.

prose.def: The quality of piety, holiness, and righteous devotion toward God, consistently paired with righteousness in both NT occurrences.
prose.article: ὁσιότης describes a God-directed holiness or piety—living rightly toward God. prose.def: A correlative relative pronoun meaning 'as much/many/long as,' 'all who,' or 'whatever/everything,' expressing full extent, quantity, or the complete membership of a group.
prose.article: ὅσος is a correlative relative pronoun that points to quantity, extent, or the full membership of a group — 'as much as,' 'all who,' 'whatever,' 'everything that.' Its meaning shifts heavily with context, which is why 42 of its 115 New Testament occurrences are simply absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own. In the Septuagint it appears 519 times and most often stands in for the Hebrew relative אֲשֶׁר (248×), and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, as in 'how much trouble I had' or 'all else that is fitting.'
prose.caution: The word's force is highly context-dependent, with measured senses spread thinly across eight renderings and over a third of cases carrying no distinct English equivalent.

prose.def: A relative pronoun, used almost exclusively in the nominative, meaning 'who,' 'whoever,' or 'anyone who,' with a generalizing or qualitative force that varies by context and author.
prose.article: ὅστις is a flexible relative pronoun that ranges from the general "whoever, anyone who" to a plain "who" identifying a particular person or thing. In the New Testament it appears 142 times but almost only in the nominative form, and translators render it most often as "who" (38×, 41%); strikingly, in 50 of those 142 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding English with no word of its own. Classically ὅστις was distinguished from the simpler ὅς, but Moulton-Milligan note that this distinction "has worn very thin in the papyri" — an everyday dinner invitation from second-century Egypt uses ἥτις just to mean "which is the 15th."
prose.caution: The renderings vary widely and the classical ὅστις/ὅς distinction is inconsistently maintained in the NT, so the exact shade of meaning often depends on context rather than the word itself.

senseLabels: made of clay (earthen vessel, metaphorical contrast)
prose.article: ὀστράκινος describes anything made of fired clay or earthenware, and by implication something frail. prose.def: The loin or waist region of the body, used literally for the area a belt encircles and figuratively as the seat of procreative or generative power.

prose.article: ὀσφῦς literally names the loin, hip, or waist area, the part of the body you wrap a belt around — which is why it appears in phrases about girding up one's waist. The Hebrews, and the New Testament writers following them, also treated this region as the seat of generative power, so it can refer to a person's offspring or descendants. prose.def: A conjunction meaning 'when' or 'whenever,' marking an indefinite or conditional point in time — often future, but also general or iterative — when one action occurs alongside another.
senseLabels: rendered within future clause (no separate English word)
prose.article: ὅταν marks the timing of an action, most often translated "when" or "whenever," and it typically refers to events expected in an indefinite future rather than fixed dates. It appears 122 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the renderings cluster tightly around "when" (45×) and "when will" (31×), with several others reflecting English's habit of folding the future tense into the phrasing. Built from ὅτε ("when") plus ἄν, it carries a conditional, open-ended flavor; the everyday papyri show the same usage, as in a first-century letter promising "whenever you want to borrow anything from me, I at once give in."
prose.caution: About 20 of 122 occurrences leave no distinct English word of their own, so the sense breakdown reflects translators' phrasing choices as much as the word itself.

Sense 3 ('will,' 10%) reflects occurrences where ὅταν is absorbed into future-tense English renderings without a clear 'when' marker — the definition does not account for how the conjunction disappears into the surrounding clause structure.

The definition omits the conditional/hypothetical nuance ('whenever' in the sense of 'if and when') that Abbott-Smith, Strong's, and the papyri all highlight as central to the particle's force. The word ὅταν is not merely temporal but carries modal conditionality from the ἄν component.

receipts.how: This beatitude uses ὅταν in a gnomic, general-condition sense ('Blessed are you whenever people insult you'), demonstrating the conditional/iterative nuance the definition underweights by calling it merely a future time-marker.

prose.article: ὅτε is a common temporal particle that points to the time at which an event occurs, rendered "when" in the overwhelming majority of cases (67×, 89% in the Byzantine NT). A few times it shades into "after" or "once" (4×) when one event follows another. Note that the listed renderings "Jesus," "came," and "these" aren't meanings of ὅτε itself — they come from neighboring words in the sentence, and the word is absorbed into the phrasing without its own English equivalent 30 times out of 105. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, including an amusing letter where a man writes his estranged wife counting the days "from when" they last bathed together.
prose.caution: The "Jesus," "came," and "these" renderings reflect translation phrasing of surrounding words, not separate meanings of ὅτε.

prose.def: A conjunction meaning 'that' (introducing reported speech or thought), 'because' or 'for' (giving a reason), or functioning as a direct-quotation marker with no English equivalent.

prose.article: ὅτι is one of the most common little connectors in the New Testament, appearing 1281 times, and it does two main jobs: it introduces what someone sees, knows, or says ("that"), and it gives a reason ("because" or "for"). Most of the measured renderings beyond these two are really ὅτι getting absorbed into surrounding English phrasing rather than carrying its own word — in fact it has no separate English word 319 times out of 1281. In the Greek Old Testament it appears a staggering 3346 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew word כִּי (2461×), which does the same double duty. One notable wrinkle: ὅτι can also stand untranslated right before a direct quotation, working almost like an opening quotation mark.
prose.caution: The many "senses" with low percentages are mostly artifacts of English phrasing absorbing the word, not distinct meanings — its real range is the simple "that"/"because" pair.

prose.def: The plain, factual word for "not" or "no," denying that something is true or real.
prose.article: This is Greek's basic, absolute negative — the everyday way to say "not" or "no" about something real. It is overwhelmingly translated simply "not" (904 of 1,637 times, 73%), with the rest being grammatical variations like "did not," "do not," or a standalone "no." senseLabels: [absorbed into phrasing — no English equivalent rendered]
prose.article: οὖν is one of the most common connecting particles in the New Testament, appearing 523 times in the Byzantine text, and its exact force shifts with context. The measured renderings cluster around three ideas: drawing a conclusion ("so," 31%; "therefore," 23%) and marking simple sequence or resumption of a story ("then," 29%). Notably, in 159 of 523 cases the word is absorbed into English phrasing with no word of its own, since it often just smooths the flow of a narrative. The everyday papyri confirm this range: one letter uses it for plain "therefore" ("I beg you, therefore, my lord father, write me a letter").

In the Septuagint it appears 163 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew אֹ֫זֶן ("ear") 115 times; the everyday papyri capture both the literal sense and a vivid idiom, with one Oxyrhynchus document (A.D. 186) using "I turned a deaf ear to him" much like Acts 7:57.

The repeated Revelation formula 'he who has an ear, let him hear' across 8 occurrences shows the metaphorical sense is pervasive and well-supported by the definition's framing.

audit.author_note: Revelation uses the singular 'ear' formula 8 times in the same stereotyped call to spiritual attentiveness, while Matthew and Luke use it in the Synoptic tradition and also record physical ear references (e.g. LUK 22:50), suggesting consistent usage across authors with no significant theological divergence.

prose.def: A person's property, wealth, or estate — the material possessions or inheritance share one owns (Luke 15:12–13 only).
prose.article: οὐσία means a person's property, wealth, or estate — the things one owns. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:12-13), where the younger son asks for and then squanders his share of the family estate. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense vividly: documents from Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt use οὐσία for landed estates, including 'the estate of Julia Augusta' and its olive-yards.
prose.caution: The two NT translation labels ('son' and 'journeyed') reflect the surrounding phrases rather than the word itself, which consistently means property; the word appears only twice in the NT.

prose.def: A negative particle meaning 'neither,' 'nor,' 'not,' or 'or,' used to link or extend negations, often in paired οὔτε...οὔτε constructions.
prose.article: οὔτε is a linking particle used to string together negatives, most often in the paired pattern "neither...nor." It's a flexible connector translated as "nor" (17×), "or" (13×), "neither nor" (11×), or simply "neither" (7×), and in 35 of its 94 appearances it gets absorbed into the phrasing without a separate English word of its own. It was common, ordinary speech: a first-century papyrus loan document uses it just as the New Testament does, in the line "neither I nor any one else having the right to expel you."

issues: The definition describes οὔτε solely as a 'connecting word that joins items in a list,' but its most important grammatical function is as a negative correlative particle, often in paired οὔτε...οὔτε constructions, not merely a list-connector.

The 'or' sense (22% of occurrences) is broadly correct as a translation rendering but the definition does not explain why οὔτε sometimes yields 'or' — it appears after implicit negation, which a careful reader needs to understand.
The definition omits the 'not' sense (sense 5), which while small (3%) does appear in the corpus (LUK 7:9, ACT 24:12) and represents οὔτε functioning closer to a simple negation.

The supporting article says 35 of 94 occurrences are 'absorbed into phrasing without a separate English word,' but this is not flagged or explained in the definition itself, which could mislead readers who encounter those verses.
The definition's framing ('joins items in a list') is too narrow; οὔτε frequently operates in extended theological arguments and emphatic double-negative constructions, not just item lists.

receipts.how: Paul's sweeping paired negations ('neither death nor life... neither... nor...') confirm the core οὔτε...οὔτε 'neither...nor' function the definition describes.

Rendered 'or' in a negated context ('not forgiven...in this age or in the age to come'), showing how οὔτε yields 'or' rather than 'nor' after implicit negation — a nuance the definition does not address.
Translated simply as 'not,' demonstrating the sense-5 simple negation function that the definition omits entirely.

audit.author_note: Paul uses οὔτε most extensively in sustained theological argument with emphatic paired constructions (ROM 8:38–39; GAL 5:6), while Revelation deploys it in visionary declarations (16×), suggesting the particle carries different rhetorical weight across authors.

prose.def: The Greek demonstrative pronoun 'this/these,' used to point out a nearby person or thing, and also functioning as a personal pronoun ('he,' 'she,' 'they') or driving set phrases like 'for this reason.'
prose.article: This is the everyday Greek demonstrative pronoun "this/these," used to point at someone or something near at hand or just mentioned. It's enormously common—1,408 times in the Byzantine New Testament—and most often simply renders as "this" (65%) or "these" (16%), though in 416 cases it gets absorbed into English phrasing with no word of its own. In the Septuagint it stands behind several Hebrew demonstratives, chiefly זֶה (932×) and זֹאת (540×), and the papyri show it filling out common stock phrases like "on this account" (διὰ τοῦτο) and "for this reason" (ἐκ τούτου).

audit.author_note: John uses οὗτος with notable theological density — particularly in ὁ λόγος οὗτος and the ἐκ τούτου idiom (JOH 6:66) — while Luke-Acts deploys it heavily in narrative identification of persons; ordinary readers of John may miss the pronoun's role in doctrinal apposition that Johannine usage exploits.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'in this way,' 'thus,' 'likewise,' or 'so also,' pointing to how something is done or drawing a comparison with what precedes or follows.
prose.article: οὕτω (more commonly spelled οὕτως) is a workhorse adverb meaning "in this way" or "thus," used to point either back to what was just said or forward to what comes next. It is extremely common — 212 times across 21 books in the Byzantine text — and so woven into the flow of a sentence that 156 of those occurrences don't get a separate English word at all. In the Septuagint it appears 685 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew כֵּן ("so, thus," 311×), and everyday Koine papyri show the same usage, as in a letter phrase "this being so" (τούτων δὲ οὕτως ἐχόντων).

issues: The current definition emphasizes the pointing function ('as just described or about to be described') but the measured senses show 'also/likewise' (21%) and 'in the same way' (16%) together account for 37% of occurrences — these comparative/additive senses are not adequately captured by 'in this way or thus' alone
Sense label 1 is listed as 'way' in the measured data but the definition and article label it 'in this way' — minor mismatch in label precision

The supporting article's claim that 156 of 212 occurrences have no separate English word conflicts with the sense frequency data, which assigns English renderings to all four senses; the absorbed-into-phrasing figure needs clarification so readers are not confused
The sense label 2 'also, likewise' in the current definition partially covers the measured 'also' sense but 'likewise' leans toward sense 3 ('same way'), blurring two distinct senses

receipts.how: Illustrates the core 'in this way' sense (sense 1), where Jesus points forward to how his followers should let their light shine — a clean anaphoric/cataphoric use the definition handles well.

Illustrates the 'also' sense (sense 2, 21% of occurrences): 'even so, when you see these things,' functioning as a comparative particle rather than a simple manner adverb — a use the definition underrepresents.

Illustrates the 'same' sense (sense 4, 11%): 'do not even the tax collectors the same?' — where the adverb functions predicatively rather than as a manner adverb, a syntactic role confirmed by the 24 predicate occurrences in the Macula data.

audit.author_note: James uses the word 9 times (proportionally high for a short letter) in wisdom-instruction contexts where 'in the same way' or 'so also' carries ethical comparative force, while Paul in 1 Corinthians (31×) frequently uses it in logical argumentation to draw inferences, suggesting readers of those books may need awareness of both manner and comparative nuances.

prose.def: A strengthened form of 'not,' meaning 'not at all' or 'certainly not,' used both as a plain emphatic negative and in rhetorical questions expecting a 'yes' answer.
prose.article: οὐχί is a strengthened version of the ordinary Greek "no" (οὐ), adding emphasis—think "not at all" rather than a plain "not." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 56 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "not" in 68% of cases, though 16 of those 56 occurrences get absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own. Its most distinctive use, noted by Abbott-Smith, is in questions that expect a "yes" answer (like Latin nonne), as in "Do not even the tax collectors do the same?" The everyday Koine papyri confirm both this question-form and a plainer negative use.

Sense label 3 'no too' is awkward and opaque for ordinary readers; it appears to reflect a mechanical rendering rather than a meaningful gloss

prose.def: A person who owes something to another—literally a debtor, figuratively someone under obligation or duty, or (in Luke) a sinner against God.
senseLabels: one who is obligated (moral or covenantal duty)
one who owes a literal debt (debtor)
one who has sinned against God (Aramaism, LUK 13:4)
prose.article: This word comes from the verb "to owe" (G3784) and ranges from a literal financial debtor to anyone under an obligation or duty. In the Byzantine New Testament's 7 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it as being "obligated" (3×, 50%), with "debtors" twice (33%) and "obligation" once. A striking witness is a Christian amulet from around the sixth century A.D. that preserves the Lord's Prayer petition asking God to forgive us as we forgive "our debtors," showing how naturally this everyday word carried both monetary and spiritual weight.
prose.caution: Several lexicons note a figurative sense of "sinner" against God (an Aramaism, e.g. Luke 13:4), but that sense does not appear in the measured Byzantine renderings here.

'Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors' shows the literal financial/moral debtor sense and matches the 'debtors' rendering (33% of occurrences).

audit.author_note: Paul (Romans, Galatians) uses the word almost exclusively for moral or covenantal obligation, while Luke 13:4 employs it in the Semitic sense of 'sinner against God,' a distinction that matters for readers moving between authors.

prose.def: Something owed to another person: a literal monetary debt, a civic or relational duty, or specifically the conjugal obligation spouses owe each other.
prose.article: ὀφειλή covers what one person owes another, ranging from a concrete sum of money to a moral obligation. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, split evenly: once as a literal "summoned debt" (Matthew 18:32) and once as what is "due" to others (Romans 13:7). Tellingly, although older lexicons claimed the word was rare outside the New Testament, the papyri show it turning up frequently in everyday business documents in the plain sense of "debt"—including a loan record from 9 B.C.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin, with only 2 Byzantine occurrences, so the sense range rests heavily on supporting papyri and lexicons.

prose.def: Something owed: either sins pictured as debts owed to God (Matthew), or wages owed as a matter of right to a worker (Romans).
senseLabels: sins as debts owed to God

prose.article: ὀφείλημα is anything owed, and the New Testament uses it both ways in its two appearances: a debt that doubles as a metaphor for sin (Matthew 6:12) and a plain obligation that is owed and must be repaid (Romans 4:4). The everyday Koine papyri confirm the literal sense vividly—one document from 262 BC promises to hand over the remainder "as a debt," and an Oxyrhynchus papyrus even distinguishes "debts recorded and unrecorded." In the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew word for a loan or claim, keeping the same financial flavor that lets it serve as a picture of sin we owe.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences split evenly between the two senses, the evidence base is thin.

Shows where the definition needs sharpening: the context is wages owed to a worker, a concrete financial/legal obligation, not a general moral duty—'obligation due' undersells this specificity.

prose.article: At its root ὀφείλω means to owe a debt, and that literal sense shows up in everyday Koine — a Will from 285 BC uses it of children responsible for their parents' debts. In the New Testament the word leans heavily toward the figurative meaning of being under obligation, which is why translators most often render it "ought" (6 of 35 times, 43% of the visible cases). The remaining 21 of 35 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew נָשָׁא, the language of lending and owing.
prose.caution: Because 21 of its 35 occurrences are blended into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, the measured sense breakdown rests on a fairly small visible sample.

prose.def: An indeclinable exclamation expressing a wish — 'I wish' or 'if only' — ranging from a fruitless longing to a genuinely practicable desire depending on the tense of the following verb.
senseLabels: how I wish (ironic exclamation, aorist indicative follows)
prose.article: ὄφελον is an exclamation meaning "I wish" or "if only," used to introduce a heartfelt desire, sometimes one the speaker knows cannot or will not happen. It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "wish" twice, "how I wish" once, and within an "already"-phrase once (2 Corinthians 11:1). The word turns up in everyday Koine too: a papyrus letter from a slave to her ailing master reads "would that I could fly and come and greet you." Grammatically it is a frozen verb form (an unaugmented aorist of ὀφείλω, "to owe") that came to function purely as a wish-word.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin — only 4 New Testament occurrences — and Abbott-Smith notes the wish ranges from fruitless to practicable depending on the verb tense that follows.

issues: Sense 3 ('would that, already') is misleading: at 2CO 11:1 the BSB renders it with 'already' as part of a wish-phrase ('I wish you would already bear with me'), but labeling it 'already' as a standalone sense conflates an adverb in the context with the function of ὄφελον itself, which remains a wish-particle throughout

Abbott-Smith's distinction between fruitless and practicable wishes (depending on following indicative tense: aorist, imperfect, or future) is mentioned only in the caution, not the main definition, leaving ordinary readers with the impression the wish is always hopeless

The syntactic role data shows ὄφελον functions vocatively (4×) — exclamatory/interjective — which the definition captures informally but does not make explicit; calling it a 'particle' is close but Abbott-Smith and Dodson both classify it as an indeclinable frozen verb form, and the definition should reflect that
Sense label 3 should be revised to reflect that '2CO 11:1' involves an imperfect indicative following ὄφελον, not a semantically distinct 'already' sense

receipts.how: Illustrates a practicable wish (future indicative follows), confirming the definition's 'if only' framing but contradicting any implication the wish is always hopeless or fruitless.
Illustrates a clearly ironic, fruitless wish (aorist indicative follows), the core sense the definition emphasizes — 'I wish that you did indeed reign.'
Shows ὄφελον with an imperfect indicative where 'already' belongs to the following clause, not to ὄφελον itself, demonstrating that labeling sense 3 as 'already' misattributes the adverb's role.

audit.author_note: Paul uses ὄφελον across three letters (1CO, 2CO, GAL) with both ironic-fruitless and genuinely practicable force, while Revelation's single use (REV 3:15) is a straightforward divine wish with no irony, suggesting readers of Revelation should not assume the hopeless connotation the definition foregrounds.

prose.def: The profit, gain, or practical advantage that something actually yields; used in rhetorical questions to challenge whether something is worth anything at all.

prose.article: ὄφελος refers to the practical advantage or benefit that something yields — the "good" it does or the profit it brings. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice in James (2:14, 2:16) asking what good faith is without works, and once in 1 Corinthians 15:32 asking what use Paul's struggle would be if the dead are not raised. Notably, it shows up in everyday Koine papyri with exactly this sense, as in an Oxyrhynchus letter saying it is "of no use" if someone arrives too late to help.
prose.caution: This word is rare, with only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint appearance, so its measured range is thin.

prose.def: To trouble, harass, or vex someone; in NT usage always of people afflicted by unclean spirits, possibly with a medical nuance.
senseLabels: to be troubled or harassed (by unclean spirits)
prose.article: ὀχλέω comes from ὄχλος ("crowd") and originally meant to mob or crowd around, then broadened to mean simply to trouble, vex, or disturb. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice (Luke 6:18, Acts 5:16), both times of people troubled by unclean spirits, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within phrases describing "those" who were afflicted. Everyday papyri show it had a thoroughly ordinary sense too — one letter pleads "don't worry the people of Sambas" — though some scholars detect a more technical, medical nuance in Acts 5:16.

audit.author_note: John uses ὄψις both for a judgment based on outward appearance (7:24) and a literal face wrapped in cloth (11:44); Revelation uses it for a visionary, glorified face—readers of Revelation may need to know the word carries the same basic 'face/appearance' meaning in an apocalyptic, visionary register.

why: ὀψώνιον occurs 4 times in the Byzantine (Majority) New Testament, across 4 books.

The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “serves” in 2 of those places (50%), e.g. 1 Corinthians 9:7; 2 Corinthians 11:8. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 100% of the same verses.
Moulton–Milligan documents this word in everyday papyri and inscriptions, anchoring the meaning in ordinary Koine usage outside the New Testament.
Moderate confidence: limited occurrences — the range shown is attested but may be incomplete.

prose.def: Compensation or wages owed for service rendered, whether military pay, general support, or metaphorically the due consequence of one's deeds.
senseLabels: provisions or support for one rendering service (general)
prose.article: ὀψώνιον means the pay or wages owed for service, and it carries a military flavor from its origins—the rations and stipend given to soldiers. Across its 4 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it around the idea of serving or wages, as when John the Baptist tells soldiers to be content with their wages (Luke 3:14) and when Paul declares that the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). A nice historical detail: Moulton-Milligan note this word was "banned by the Atticists" as too colloquial, yet it became very common in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Polybius even records soldiers receiving two obols a day as their ὀψώνιον.
prose.caution: With only 4 occurrences the sense breakdown rests on thin data, though the lexicons agree closely on its meaning.

issues: Sense label 1 'pay for military service' and label 2 'soldiers' wages' are redundant and do not match the corpus-measured senses, which distinguish a general 'serves/support' sense (50%) from the specifically military sense (25%)
The dominant measured sense (50%, 1CO 9:7 and 2CO 11:8) is rendered 'serves' or general support/provision, which the current definition and sense labels underweight relative to the military framing
Abbott-Smith explicitly distinguishes two senses—(1) provisions/soldiers' pay and (2) wages/hire generally—but the current three sense labels collapse these poorly and mislabel the top sense
The definition's emphasis on 'originally a soldier's rations' foregrounds etymology over actual NT usage distribution, potentially misleading readers about the word's predominant sense in Paul

receipts.how: Paul uses ὀψώνιον for the general support owed to anyone who serves (a soldier, a vineyard worker, a shepherd), showing the word functions beyond strictly military pay and represents the dominant sense at 50% of occurrences.
John the Baptist's command to soldiers to be content with their ὀψώνιον clearly anchors the military-wages sense and corroborates the definition's core meaning.

Paul's 'the wages of sin is death' extends ὀψώνιον metaphorically to a non-military, theological reward-for-service context, confirming the general 'wages/hire' sense the definition only partially captures.

audit.author_note: Paul uses ὀψώνιον in three of four occurrences: twice for general compensation owed to anyone rendering service (1CO 9:7; 2CO 11:8) and once in a striking theological metaphor (ROM 6:23), while Luke's single use (3:14) is the only strictly military context; a reader of Paul needs the broader 'compensation for service' sense more than the military framing.
